claim: The tracking microscope collects brightfield images of individual animals at a frequency of 20 Hz and resolution of 1.4 um/pixel.
source: The microscope, which shares several design features with previously described microscopy platforms (Yemini et al., 2013; see also Faumont and Lockery, 2006; Nguyen et al., 2016; Venkatachalam et al., 2016), collects brightfield images of individual animals (Figure 1B) at a frequency of 20 Hz and resolution of 1.4 um/pixel, which is sufficient to capture the most rapid and small-scale movements of C. elegans, such as pharyngeal motion (Avery and You, 2012; Lockery et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the imaging frequency and resolution specifications of the tracking microscope, with citations to support the claim that these specifications are sufficient for capturing C. elegans movements.

claim: A closed-loop tracking system reliably keeps animals in view over hours or days.
source: A closed-loop tracking system reliably keeps animals in view over hours or days, while live data compression makes storage of approximately 1.7 million images per animal per day feasible.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the tracking system's capability to maintain animals in view for extended periods.

claim: Live data compression makes storage of approximately 1.7 million images per animal per day feasible.
source: A closed-loop tracking system reliably keeps animals in view over hours or days, while live data compression makes storage of approximately 1.7 million images per animal per day feasible.
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative measure of the data storage capacity enabled by compression.

claim: Egg-laying events were predominant during rapid forward locomotion.
source: Egg-laying events were predominant during rapid forward locomotion, while defecation events were most commonly observed during slow or reverse movement.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the relationship between egg-laying and locomotion velocity based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Defecation events were most commonly observed during slow or reverse movement.
source: Egg-laying events were predominant during rapid forward locomotion, while defecation events were most commonly observed during slow or reverse movement.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the relationship between defecation and locomotion velocity based on analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Body postures that animals express co-vary considerably with velocity.
source: From these histograms and from the set of most common body postures, it is evident that the postures that animals express co-vary considerably with velocity, suggesting that animals sample different body postures at different velocities (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript states this relationship based on analysis of posture histograms and eigenworm projections shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Egg-laying and defecation events each occur during stereotyped posture and locomotion changes.
source: These analyses revealed many of the same relationships between the behavioral outputs, but also showed that egg-laying and defecation events each occur during stereotyped posture and locomotion changes, as has been previously reported (Collins et al., 2016; Hardaker et al., 2001; Nagy et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding based on event-triggered average analysis, with citations to previous reports of similar observations.

claim: A model with nine hidden states provided the best fit to the recorded data based on Bayesian information criteria.
source: Based on Bayesian information criteria (BIC) estimates, a model with nine hidden states provided the best fit to the recorded data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the optimal number of hidden states determined by BIC analysis, with reference to supporting figure.

claim: One behavioral state consisted of high forward velocity, low angular speed and typically lasted from tens of seconds to many minutes, equivalent to the previously defined roaming state.
source: One of these behavioral states consisted of high forward velocity, low angular speed and typically lasted from tens of seconds to many minutes (Figure 2E). Based on these parameters, this state is equivalent to the previously defined roaming state (Figure 2E; labeled 'Roam') (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Flavell et al., 2013; Fujiwara et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of this state and identifies it as roaming based on comparison to previous literature.

claim: Animals traveled at lower velocities during the other eight states but maintained high pumping and defecation rates in each.
source: Animals traveled at lower velocities during the other eight states, but, in contrast to quiescence/sleep states, they maintained high pumping and defecation rates in each (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the behavioral characteristics of the eight dwelling sub-modes.

claim: Quiescence states were almost never observed under the recording conditions used (only five ~20 s bouts identified in ~180 hr of data).
source: Quiescence states were not recovered from this analysis because this state was almost never observed under our recording conditions (only five ~20 s bouts identified in ~180 hr of data; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data on the rarity of quiescence states under their experimental conditions.

claim: Animals displayed stereotyped body postures in each of the dwelling sub-modes that were significantly different from one another.
source: Moreover, animals displayed stereotyped body postures in each of the dwelling sub-modes that were significantly different from one another (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding with reference to supporting figures and video showing the distinct postures.

claim: The average duration of each dwelling sub-mode was ~10 s.
source: The average duration of each sub-mode was ~10 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B) and animals transitioned between them in a non-random fashion: the transition rates between many sub-modes were close to zero, whereas other transition rates were quite high (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific quantitative measure of sub-mode duration with reference to supporting figures.

claim: Animals transitioned between dwelling sub-modes in a non-random fashion.
source: The average duration of each sub-mode was ~10 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–B) and animals transitioned between them in a non-random fashion: the transition rates between many sub-modes were close to zero, whereas other transition rates were quite high (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the structured nature of transitions between sub-modes based on analysis of transition rates.

claim: Posture sequences generated by the posture-HMM were a significantly better match to sequences from actual animals compared to alternative continuous models.
source: Based on this criterion, the posture sequences generated by the posture-HMM were a significantly better match to the sequences from actual animals, compared to the alternative models (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: The manuscript states the result of a comparison between the HMM and alternative models, with reference to supporting figure.

claim: Egg-laying rates were highest during roaming, whereas the dwelling sub-modes had smaller, but significant, differences in their egg-laying rates.
source: Egg-laying rates were highest during roaming, whereas the dwelling sub-modes had smaller, but significant, differences in their egg-laying rates.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the pattern of egg-laying rates across behavioral states.

claim: Defecation rates were significantly different between the nine states, but feeding rates were the same across the states.
source: Defecation rates were also significantly different between the nine states, but feeding rates were the same across the states (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the differences in defecation and feeding rates across states.

claim: Animals displayed a universally higher egg-laying rate during roaming compared to dwelling, even when matched for velocity.
source: While there was a positive correlation between velocity and egg-laying rate within each state, we observed a universally higher egg-laying rate during roaming compared to dwelling, even when matched for velocity (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of an analysis controlling for velocity to isolate the state-dependent effect on egg-laying.

claim: Serotonin-deficient tph-1 mutants displayed reduced dwelling, higher speeds during roaming, reduced feeding, and fewer egg-laying events.
source: Serotonin-deficient tph-1 mutants displayed reduced dwelling, higher speeds during roaming, reduced feeding, and fewer egg-laying events, as has been previously described (Figure 3A–B; Avery and You, 2012; Flavell et al., 2013; Hobson et al., 2006; Horvitz et al., 1982).
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral phenotypes of tph-1 mutants with citations to previous reports.

claim: The increase in egg-laying rates during roaming states was largely intact in tph-1 mutants, suggesting that serotonin is dispensable for this form of motor program coupling.
source: However, the increase in egg-laying rates during roaming states was largely intact, suggesting that serotonin is dispensable for this form of motor program coupling.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the tph-1 mutant data to conclude that serotonin is not required for coupling egg-laying to roaming.

claim: pdfr-1 mutants spent less time roaming, traveled at lower velocity while roaming, and did not bias their egg-laying to the state as robustly as wild-type animals.
source: pdfr-1 mutants, deficient in PDF neuropeptide signaling, displayed a broad defect in roaming states: they spent less time roaming, traveled at lower velocity while roaming, and did not bias their egg-laying to the state as robustly as wild-type animals.
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral phenotypes of pdfr-1 mutants.

claim: The pdfr-1 mutant egg-laying phenotype may be part of a general deficit in their ability to display roaming states rather than a specific deficit in motor program coupling.
source: Thus, although pdfr-1 mutants are defective in locomotion and egg-laying during roaming, this may be part of a general deficit in their ability to display roaming states (Flavell et al., 2013), rather than a specific deficit in motor program coupling.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the pdfr-1 mutant phenotype with citation to previous work.

claim: tdc-1 mutants that are defective in tyramine and octopamine displayed increased time in the roaming state but their egg-laying rates were still higher while roaming.
source: tdc-1 mutants that are defective in tyramine and octopamine displayed increased time in the roaming state. However, their egg-laying rates were still higher while roaming.
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral phenotypes of tdc-1 mutants.

claim: tbh-1 mutants defective in octopamine synthesis showed a mild increase in their roaming velocity, but no deficit in egg-laying.
source: tbh-1 mutants defective in octopamine synthesis showed a mild increase in their roaming velocity, but no deficit in egg-laying.
evidence: The manuscript describes the behavioral phenotypes of tbh-1 mutants.

claim: Dopamine-deficient cat-2 mutants displayed a striking loss of coupling between egg-laying and the roaming state.
source: In contrast, dopamine-deficient cat-2 mutants displayed a striking loss of coupling between egg-laying and the roaming state.
evidence: The manuscript describes the key phenotype of cat-2 mutants.

claim: cat-2 mutants displayed robust roaming states but their egg-laying rate was dramatically reduced during roaming.
source: Although these animals displayed robust roaming states, their egg-laying rate was dramatically reduced during roaming (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specific behavioral phenotype of cat-2 mutants.

claim: cat-2 mutants' egg-laying rate during the dwelling state was unaltered.
source: In contrast, their egg-laying rate during the dwelling state was unaltered.
evidence: The manuscript describes the state-specific nature of the cat-2 mutant phenotype.

claim: cat-2 animals travel at a higher velocity than wild-type animals while roaming but still display the same postures.
source: cat-2 animals travel at a higher velocity than wild-type animals while roaming (Figure 3A), but still display the same postures (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that they are not broadly defective in the locomotor components of roaming (Sawin et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript describes the locomotion and posture characteristics of cat-2 mutants with citation to previous work.

claim: There is only a modest reduction in egg-laying overall in cat-2 mutant animals because they have unaltered egg-laying rates during dwelling, which is the more prevalent state.
source: Because they have unaltered egg-laying rates during dwelling, which is the more prevalent state, there is only a modest reduction in egg-laying overall in these mutant animals (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript explains why the overall egg-laying phenotype is modest despite the roaming-specific deficit.

claim: cat-2 mutants were not recovered as egg-laying defective (egl) in forward genetic screens, consistent with them not being broadly defective in egg-laying.
source: This suggests that they are not broadly defective in egg-laying, a finding that is consistent with the fact that they were not recovered as egg-laying defective (egl) in forward genetic screens.
evidence: The manuscript uses the absence of cat-2 from previous genetic screens as supporting evidence for their interpretation.

claim: A second, independent null allele of cat-2 caused a similar phenotype to the first allele.
source: To ensure that this motor coupling phenotype was caused by the loss of the cat-2 gene, we examined a second, independent null allele of cat-2 and found that it caused a similar phenotype (Figure 3C–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of a second allele to confirm the genetic basis of the phenotype.

claim: Rescue of cat-2 expression in the mutant via a transgene restored higher egg-laying rates during roaming.
source: In addition, we rescued cat-2 expression in the mutant via a transgene and found that this restored higher egg-laying rates during roaming (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes a genetic rescue experiment confirming the role of cat-2.

claim: Dopamine is necessary for proper coupling of egg-laying to the roaming state.
source: These data suggest that dopamine is necessary for proper coupling of egg-laying to the roaming state and highlights the value of simultaneously quantifying multiple ongoing motor programs within the animal.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the cat-2 mutant analysis.

claim: egl-1 mutant animals showed a dramatic reduction in egg-laying during both roaming and dwelling states.
source: To test for potential floor effects, we recorded mutant animals with deficits in the egg-laying motor circuit (egl-1). These animals showed a dramatic reduction in egg-laying during both roaming and dwelling states (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that floor effects do not account for the cat-2 phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript describes the egl-1 mutant phenotype as a control to rule out floor effects.

claim: None of the single dopamine receptor mutants showed any egg-laying phenotypes.
source: To further characterize the dopaminergic pathway that couples egg-laying and locomotion during roaming, we examined mutants lacking each of the seven known dopamine receptors in C. elegans (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2). None of these single mutants showed any egg-laying phenotypes.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of screening single dopamine receptor mutants.

claim: Mutant animals lacking the two D2-like dopamine receptors, dop-2 and dop-3, displayed reduced egg-laying rates during roaming, but not dwelling, closely matching the cat-2 mutant phenotype.
source: However, we found that mutant animals lacking the two D2-like dopamine receptors, dop-2 and dop-3, displayed reduced egg-laying rates during roaming, but not dwelling, closely matching the cat-2 mutant phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript describes the phenotype of the dop-2;dop-3 double mutant.

claim: dop-2 and dop-3 act together to regulate egg-laying during the roaming state.
source: These results suggest that dop-2 and dop-3 act together to regulate egg-laying during the roaming state.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the dop-2;dop-3 double mutant analysis.

claim: dop-2;dop-3 double mutants display normal velocities during roaming but have dramatically reduced egg-laying rates during roaming.
source: However, an analysis of velocity and egg-laying rates across the receptor mutants suggests that this is not the case: dop-2;dop-3 double mutants display normal velocities during roaming (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), but have dramatically reduced egg-laying rates during roaming (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript uses this observation to argue against an indirect effect of dopamine on egg-laying via locomotion changes.

claim: Eggs laid during roaming were farther apart from other eggs compared to those laid during dwelling.
source: As expected, we found that eggs laid during roaming were farther apart from other eggs compared to those laid during dwelling (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of analyzing egg spacing.

claim: Animals dispersed their eggs more during roaming than dwelling based on analysis of egg distribution across explored area.
source: This analysis also revealed a greater dispersal of eggs during roaming (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of analyzing egg dispersal across the explored area.

claim: Dopamine-defective mutants (both cat-2 and dop-2;dop-3) displayed a significant reduction in egg dispersal.
source: Moreover, dopamine-defective mutants (both cat-2 and dop-2;dop-3) displayed a significant reduction in egg dispersal (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the egg dispersal phenotype of dopamine pathway mutants.

claim: cat-2 and dop-2;dop-3 mutants both laid a higher fraction of their eggs during dwelling, as compared to roaming.
source: Consistent with these results, cat-2 and dop-2; dop-3 mutants both laid a higher fraction of their eggs during dwelling, as compared to roaming (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the distribution of eggs across states in dopamine pathway mutants.

claim: The coupling of egg-laying to the roaming state increases the dispersal of eggs across a food source, which could have important implications for the survival of an animal's progeny.
source: These data suggest that the coupling of egg-laying to the roaming state increases the dispersal of eggs across a food source, which could have important implications for the survival of an animal's progeny.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the egg dispersal findings in terms of potential adaptive significance.

claim: Exposing dat-1::GtACR2 animals to light caused them to display lower egg-laying rates that persisted until the light was terminated.
source: Exposing these animals to light caused them to display lower egg-laying rates that persisted until the light was terminated (Figure 5A; additional controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of optogenetic silencing of dopaminergic neurons.

claim: Silencing of dopaminergic neurons reduced egg-laying rates while animals were roaming, but only had a mild, non-significant effect during dwelling.
source: This analysis indicated that the silencing of dopaminergic neurons reduced egg-laying rates while animals were roaming, but only had a mild, non-significant effect during dwelling.
evidence: The manuscript describes the state-specific effects of optogenetic silencing.

claim: Dopaminergic neuron silencing had no significant effects on feeding or defecation, and only a small, transient effect on locomotion.
source: We examined the other behaviors automatically quantified by the tracking microscopes but observed no significant effects of dopaminergic neuron silencing on feeding or defecation, and only a small, transient effect on locomotion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes the specificity of the optogenetic silencing effects.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons function to acutely promote egg-laying in adult roaming animals.
source: These data corroborate our genetic findings and suggest that dopaminergic neurons function to acutely promote egg-laying in adult roaming animals.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the optogenetic silencing experiments.

claim: Activation of dat-1::CoChR for three minute durations caused animals to display elevated egg-laying rates.
source: Activation of dat-1::CoChR for three minute durations caused animals to display elevated egg-laying rates (Figure 5C; minimal effects on velocity, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and F–H; additional controls in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of optogenetic activation of dopaminergic neurons.

claim: The increase in egg-laying rate from dat-1::CoChR activation persisted throughout the period of light exposure and was not necessarily time-locked to the moment of light onset.
source: This increase in the rate of egg-laying persisted throughout the period of light exposure and was not necessarily time-locked to the moment of light onset.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal characteristics of the optogenetic activation effect.

claim: Acute activation of the egg-laying motor neuron HSN is known to trigger egg-laying events within seconds of light exposure.
source: By contrast, acute activation of the egg-laying motor neuron HSN is known to trigger egg-laying events within seconds of light exposure (Emtage et al., 2012; Leifer et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on HSN activation for comparison.

claim: Increased dopaminergic neuron activity increases the frequency of egg-laying events.
source: These data suggest that increased dopaminergic neuron activity increases the frequency of egg-laying events.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Light exposure to dat-1::CoChR animals elevated egg-laying during the dwelling state, but not during roaming.
source: We found that light exposure to dat-1::CoChR animals elevated egg-laying during the dwelling state, but not during roaming (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the state-specific effects of optogenetic activation.

claim: The finding that exogenous activation of dopaminergic neurons during dwelling is sufficient to increase egg-laying argues against a model where downstream circuits only respond to dopamine during roaming, but not dwelling.
source: The finding that the exogenous activation of dopaminergic neurons during dwelling is sufficient to increase egg-laying argues against a model where downstream circuits only respond to dopamine during roaming, but not dwelling.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the optogenetic activation results to rule out a specific model.

claim: The finding that dat-1::CoChR activation does not further enhance egg-laying during roaming may reflect an occlusion effect, perhaps due to the already high egg-laying rates during roaming.
source: The finding that dat-1::CoChR activation does not further enhance egg-laying during roaming may reflect an occlusion effect, perhaps due to the already high egg-laying rates during roaming.
evidence: The manuscript offers a speculative explanation for the lack of effect during roaming.

claim: Optogenetic dopaminergic neuron silencing and activation caused the same velocity change: a transient decrease in speed at light onset and a transient increase in speed at light offset.
source: These two manipulations, which caused opposite effects on egg-laying, caused the same velocity change: a transient decrease in speed at light onset and a transient increase in speed at light offset (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the velocity effects of both optogenetic manipulations.

claim: The effects of opposing optogenetic manipulations on egg-laying cannot be plausibly explained as an indirect consequence of altering locomotion.
source: Therefore, the effects of these opposing optogenetic manipulations on egg-laying cannot be plausibly explained as an indirect consequence of altering locomotion.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the analysis of velocity changes during optogenetic manipulations.

claim: Animals have dramatically lower egg-laying rates when they are removed from their food source.
source: Animals have dramatically lower egg-laying rates when they are removed from their food source.
evidence: The manuscript states this as background for the off-food optogenetics experiment.

claim: Dopamine signaling is thought to be elevated in the presence of food.
source: Because dopamine signaling is thought to be elevated in the presence of food (Sawin et al., 2000; Tanimoto et al., 2016), we asked whether increasing dopaminergic neuron activity in the absence of food was sufficient to increase egg-laying rates.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on dopamine signaling in relation to food.

claim: Activation of dat-1::CoChR could drive animals to lay eggs in the absence of food at significantly higher rates.
source: Strikingly, we found that activation of dat-1::CoChR could drive animals to lay eggs in the absence of food at significantly higher rates (Figure 5E–F; velocity in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of optogenetic activation in the absence of food.

claim: Native dopaminergic neuron activity in adult animals increases the probability of egg-laying during roaming states.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that native dopaminergic neuron activity in adult animals increases the probability of egg-laying during roaming states, and that exogenous dopaminergic neuron activity during dwelling or in the absence of food is sufficient to enhance egg-laying rates.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the conclusions from the optogenetics experiments.

claim: Exogenous dopaminergic neuron activity during dwelling or in the absence of food is sufficient to enhance egg-laying rates.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that native dopaminergic neuron activity in adult animals increases the probability of egg-laying during roaming states, and that exogenous dopaminergic neuron activity during dwelling or in the absence of food is sufficient to enhance egg-laying rates.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the conclusions from the optogenetics experiments.

claim: The CEPD, CEPV, and ADE classes of dopaminergic neurons appeared to have static calcium levels while animals explored food and did not display dynamics that were dependent on locomotion speed.
source: The CEPD, CEPV, and ADE classes of neurons appeared to have static calcium levels while animals explored food and did not display dynamics that were dependent on locomotion speed (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the calcium imaging results for three dopaminergic neuron types.

claim: The dopaminergic PDE neurons displayed robust calcium dynamics as animals freely explored a food lawn.
source: However, the dopaminergic PDE neurons displayed robust calcium dynamics as animals freely explored a food lawn (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the calcium imaging results for PDE neurons.

claim: PDE neurons have short ciliated sensory dendrites that protrude through the cuticle along the dorsal side of the animal in the posterior section of the body.
source: PDE neurons have short ciliated sensory dendrites that protrude through the cuticle along the dorsal side of the animal in the posterior section of the body.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical features of PDE neurons.

claim: The PDE axon travels along the ventral nerve cord, from the posterior to the anterior end of the animal.
source: The PDE axon travels along the ventral nerve cord, from the posterior to the anterior end of the animal.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical features of PDE neurons.

claim: PDE is the only dopaminergic neuron whose neurite passes in close proximity to the egg-laying circuit and vulval muscles.
source: Notably, PDE is the only dopaminergic neuron whose neurite passes in close proximity to the egg-laying circuit and vulval muscles.
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical relationship between PDE and the egg-laying circuit.

claim: Fluctuations in PDE calcium levels were significantly increased during high-speed movement, particularly during roaming.
source: We found that fluctuations in PDE calcium levels were significantly increased during high-speed movement (Figure 6A), particularly during roaming (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), a relationship that resembles how animal movement is coupled to egg-laying (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between PDE activity and locomotion speed.

claim: PDE activity was highly correlated with the animal's body curvature, being most active when the dorsal body wall muscles were contracted on the posterior end of the body.
source: As animals moved, PDE activity was highly correlated with the animal's body curvature. PDE was most active when the dorsal body wall muscles were contracted on the posterior end of the body (Figure 6B shows an example; Figure 6C shows correlations).
evidence: The manuscript describes the relationship between PDE activity and body posture.

claim: The correlation between posture and PDE activity was present during roaming and dwelling.
source: This correlation between posture and PDE activity was present during roaming and dwelling (Figure 6C; Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the consistency of the posture-PDE activity correlation across states.

claim: PDE activity oscillated during roaming and was significantly elevated during a specific phase of each sinusoidal propagating wave.
source: Thus, one result of the correlation between PDE activity and body curvature was that PDE activity oscillated during roaming and was significantly elevated during a specific phase of each sinusoidal propagating wave (Figure 6D shows an example; Figure 6E shows averages).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phase-locked nature of PDE activity during roaming.

claim: PDE displayed significantly reduced dynamics during forward locomotion in the absence of food.
source: Because PDE has an exposed sensory ending, we examined whether this activity pattern was impacted by the presence of bacterial food in the environment. Indeed, we found that PDE displayed significantly reduced dynamics during forward locomotion in the absence of food (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of food presence on PDE activity.

claim: The relationships between PDE fluorescence and body posture were not observed when imaging PDE::GFP (instead of GCaMP), indicating that they were not due to motion artifacts.
source: These relationships between PDE fluorescence and body posture were not observed when imaging PDE::GFP (instead of GCaMP), indicating that they were not due to motion artifacts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The manuscript describes a control experiment ruling out motion artifacts.

claim: PDE calcium levels oscillate during forward movement on food, with a reliable activity peak during a specific phase of the forward propagating wave during roaming.
source: These data indicate that PDE calcium levels oscillate during forward movement on food, with a reliable activity peak during a specific phase of the forward propagating wave during roaming.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the PDE calcium imaging findings.

claim: Egg-laying events were strongly biased to a specific phase of the sinusoidal wave during roaming.
source: Indeed, egg-laying events were strongly biased to a specific phase of the sinusoidal wave (Figure 6F).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phase-dependence of egg-laying during roaming.

claim: The phase of maximal PDE activity overlapped with and shortly preceded the phase of maximal egg-laying.
source: Notably, the phase of maximal PDE activity overlapped with and shortly preceded the phase of maximal egg-laying.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal relationship between PDE activity and egg-laying.

claim: The postural changes that preceded egg-laying during roaming were distinct from those during dwelling, even though animals adopted similar postures in both states at the precise moment of egg-laying.
source: These postural changes that preceded egg-laying during roaming were distinct from those during that preceded egg-laying events during dwelling, even though animals adopted similar postures in both states at the precise moment of egg-laying (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript describes differences in the postural trajectories leading to egg-laying in different states.

claim: The animal's gait during roaming leads to a unique coupling of body curvature to egg-laying, in a manner that causes PDE activity to shortly precede the typical body posture for egg-laying.
source: These data indicate that the animal's gait during roaming leads to a unique coupling of body curvature to egg-laying, in a manner that causes PDE activity to shortly precede the typical body posture for egg-laying.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the relationship between PDE activity, body posture, and egg-laying.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the phase-dependence of egg-laying in dopamine-deficient cat-2 mutants.
source: To test this possibility, we examined the distribution of egg-laying events in dopamine-deficient cat-2 mutants and found that there was a significant decrease in the phase-dependence of egg-laying (Figure 6G).
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of cat-2 mutation on the phase-dependence of egg-laying.

claim: The difference in phase-dependence of egg-laying in cat-2 mutants was not due to a general change in body postures during roaming, since wild-type animals and cat-2 mutants displayed similar postures during forward propagating waves while roaming.
source: This difference was not due to a general change in body postures during roaming, since wild-type animals and cat-2 mutants displayed similar postures during forward propagating waves while roaming (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: The manuscript rules out a confounding explanation for the cat-2 mutant phenotype.

claim: The activity of dopaminergic PDE neurons is phase-locked to egg-laying events during roaming and dopamine signaling is required for proper coordination of body posture and egg-laying during roaming.
source: Together, these data suggest that the activity of dopaminergic PDE neurons is phase-locked to egg-laying events during roaming and that dopamine signaling is required for proper coordination of body posture and egg-laying during roaming.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the conclusions from the PDE calcium imaging and cat-2 mutant analysis.

claim: dat-1::CoChR activation still elevated egg-laying rates in acr-2 mutants, suggesting that cholinergic transmission in ventral cord neurons is not essential for these effects.
source: dat-1::CoChR activation still elevated egg-laying rates in acr-2 mutants, suggesting that cholinergic transmission in ventral cord neurons is not essential for these effects.
evidence: The manuscript describes the result of optogenetic activation in acr-2 mutants.

claim: dat-1::CoChR activation had a reduced effect in egl-1 and lin-39 mutants.
source: However, dat-1::CoChR activation had a reduced effect in egl-1 and lin-39 mutants and failed to elevate egg-laying rates in unc-25 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of optogenetic activation in different mutant backgrounds.

claim: dat-1::CoChR activation failed to elevate egg-laying rates in unc-25 mutants.
source: However, dat-1::CoChR activation had a reduced effect in egl-1 and lin-39 mutants and failed to elevate egg-laying rates in unc-25 mutants.
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of optogenetic activation in different mutant backgrounds.

claim: The finding that HSN and VCs are required for dopamine-induced egg-laying is not surprising, since these motor neurons are centrally involved in driving egg-laying.
source: The finding that HSN and VCs are required for dopamine-induced egg-laying is not surprising, since these motor neurons are centrally involved in driving egg-laying, but the role of GABAergic signaling in egg-laying has not been well-studied, so we examined this interaction more closely.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the requirement for HSN and VCs in the context of known egg-laying circuitry.

claim: The role of GABAergic signaling in egg-laying has not been well-studied.
